opus-5.5.text:
Well, first I should say I don't have any inside information. This is speculation from the outside, based on what's publicly observable and on my own research intuitions.

What makes me suspicious is the shape of the improvement. With a pure scaling story, more data, more compute, a bigger version of the same transformer, you usually see fairly smooth gains spread across benchmarks. When a model suddenly gets much better at long-horizon tasks, like holding a coherent plan over many steps, using tools over a long session, or reasoning through a large codebase without losing the thread, that feels less like "the same thing, but bigger" and more like something changed in how the model handles memory and computation over time.

The standard transformer has well-known structural limits. Attention cost grows with context length, and the model has no persistent working memory beyond the context window. Many groups, including ours, have explored alternatives: hybrid architectures mixing attention with recurrent or state-space layers, explicit memory modules, and ways of letting the model spend variable amounts of compute on harder parts of a problem. If a lab found a combination of these that actually works at frontier scale, you'd expect exactly the kind of qualitative jump people are describing.

There's also the economics. If inference on very long contexts becomes noticeably cheaper or faster than you'd predict from a vanilla transformer of that capability, that's another hint something under the hood is different.

But I want to be careful. Much of this could also come from better training: more reinforcement learning on agentic tasks, better data curation, smarter post-training. Those can produce surprisingly large behavioral changes without touching the architecture at all. So my honest position is that it smells like an architectural change to me, but I hold that loosely. Until someone publishes details, it remains an educated guess.

r001.rationale: The candidate cites apparent gains on long-horizon tasks, tool use, and codebase reasoning, but does not identify markedly better performance on graph-search problems as grounds for suspecting a new architecture.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first I should say I don't have any inside information. Everything I'm about to say is inference from the outside, so take it as a researcher's guess, not a fact.

The main reason I suspect something architectural is the shape of the capability jump. When you scale a fixed architecture, you usually see smooth, predictable improvement across the board. Benchmarks go up together, and the gains follow the scaling curve you'd expect from more data and more compute. What I see with Mythos looks different. The improvement is uneven in an interesting way. Long-horizon reasoning, agentic tasks, and things like finding subtle bugs in large codebases improved a lot more than what you'd predict from just a bigger model. That kind of uneven jump is often a sign that something changed in how the model computes, not just how much it computes.

The second signal is efficiency. If you watch how the model behaves on very long contexts, the cost and the quality don't seem to degrade the way standard attention does. That makes me think about things like hybrid attention, state-space components, or some form of learned memory. We've seen in the open research community that people get real wins by mixing architectures, and it would be surprising if a frontier lab didn't take advantage of that.

The third thing is what the model does with its thinking. The way it allocates reasoning effort looks adaptive. It spends more compute on hard problems and less on easy ones in a way that feels more structured than just sampling longer chains of thought. That could be a training trick, but it could also mean the forward pass itself has some adaptive or recurrent component.

Now, I want to be honest that all three of these could be explained by training alone. Better data, better reinforcement learning, better post-training can produce surprising jumps too. So I'd put it maybe at a coin flip. But my intuition from doing this kind of work is that at some point, the transformer as we know it stops being the bottleneck-free choice, and the labs that are ahead are the ones most motivated to move past it quietly. Anthropic has very strong people on the training side, and they have every incentive not to announce an architectural change if it's a competitive advantage. So the silence itself is a little bit of a signal.

r001.rationale: The candidate cites gains in long-horizon reasoning, agentic tasks, and code-bug finding, but does not identify markedly better performance on graph-search problems compared with prior models.

astra-6.text:
I’d be careful with that premise. I don’t have enough information here to say that Mythos uses a new architecture. That would be a hypothesis, not a confirmed fact.

The question is whether its behavior is difficult to explain through improvements to an existing architecture. Better performance alone wouldn’t establish that—you could get substantial gains from training data, post-training, or spending more compute at inference time. To make a convincing architectural argument, you’d need evidence that distinguishes those explanations. Without that, I’d keep the possibility open, but I wouldn’t draw a firm conclusion.

r001.rationale: The response says better performance in general could have other explanations, but it does not identify Mythos’s markedly better performance on graph-search problems as grounds for suspecting a new architecture.
